person:shawn meaike.first_money_or_break_en: Raised in a poor single-parent household, he worked as a police officer (later fired) and a social worker earning $58,000 a year before going bankrupt from a failed young home purchase. After rebuilding his credit, he secured a $1 million credit line from a local bank to develop a real estate subdivision, then founded a waste disposal company and a life insurance distribution business, snowballing them through sales skill and continuous profit reinvestment.
person:shawn meaike.zero_start_advice_en: Start from zero in sales, the industry with the lowest capital barrier, pick a product you believe in, sell relentlessly, and learn to teach others to sell. Proactively seek advice from successful people, mentors, top lawyers, and accountants, curb spending to reinvest profits into the business, face discomfort head-on, and focus on controllable solutions.

person:grant cardone.first_money_or_break_en: After quitting bad habits at age 25, he spent three and a half years working long days in sales to build his skills before entering real estate. While his first two single-family properties netted only $200 a month in cash flow, at 30 he raised $350,000 with no credit history or personal capital to buy his third deal, a 48-unit apartment complex, netting $3.7 million and transforming his wealth.
person:grant cardone.zero_start_advice_en: Eliminate idle time to avoid laziness and temptation, and build connections through networking because wealth flows through people. Do not hoard cash early on; reinvest every dollar you earn into your skills, brand, and business, then transition as soon as possible into scalable cash-flowing physical assets like real estate.

person:john morgan.first_money_or_break_en: Born into a modest family in Kentucky, he developed entrepreneurial grit from age 7 selling greeting cards and working year-round as a paperboy. After his brother was paralyzed in an accident while he was in college and failed to receive fair treatment, he decided to study law and eventually co-founded Morgan & Morgan, North America's largest personal injury law firm, with his brother and partners.
person:john morgan.zero_start_advice_en: Avoid trading hours for wages and instead choose a commission-based, high-upside platform or join a winning team. Stop using "I should have started earlier" as an excuse and plant your first tree today; stay debt-free with cash reserves, never speculate in areas you do not understand, and build long-term trust through the Golden Rule and selfless giving.

person:robert miller.first_money_or_break_en: At age 19 in college, influenced by a friend, he got into crypto early in 2015-2016 and invested $1,500 to $2,000 into Bitcoin, Ethereum, and NEO (AntShares), growing it to roughly $250,000 within four months. That first major stake enabled him to pivot into free teaching, speaking, e-commerce, and digital marketing ventures.
person:robert miller.zero_start_advice_en: Do not rely blindly on a college degree, since entrepreneurship is about solving real problems; prioritize mastering content traffic marketing, sales closing, and business cash flow. Build a personal brand continuously, reinvest early profits into self-education, quality courses, and mentor masterminds, trade money to buy back time, go deep on one core business, and choose partners strictly for shared values.

person:robert herjavec.first_money_or_break_en: Born into poverty and having fled with his parents to Canada, he entered the then-doubted internet and cybersecurity sectors at age 21 to seize an early edge. By creating value through his own effort, he eventually sold his company and made roughly $500 million in a single year (including capital gains).
person:robert herjavec.zero_start_advice_en: If starting from zero while keeping his network, he would launch an AI company focused on AI data infrastructure. If starting with zero capital at all, he would start in e-commerce to build an online brand, winning customers and connections by delivering value and positive energy.

clip:d4Yuq3iP5eI:0.first_money_or_break_en: Raised on a farm and having once lived on welfare, he landed a first major contract worth $9 million in annualized revenue that required fronting about $1 million in working capital for 30-day payment terms. He survived the first five weeks using 21% high-interest accounts receivable factoring and reinvested 100% of earnings without taking dividends.
clip:d4Yuq3iP5eI:0.zero_start_advice_en: Do not raise money from early investors empty-handed (or you will give up 51%-70% equity); instead, prove minimum revenue and business viability at low cost first. Skip paying yourself as much as possible, live minimally to snowball cash flow, build bank trust early, join non-promotional founder peer groups, stay confident, and never quit.

person:robert dugen.first_money_or_break_en: Having started out earning just 50 cents an hour, he began investing in college with $5,000 under a mentor's guidance, growing it to $3.6 million (before drawing down to $600,000 and refocusing). Later, after his son was diagnosed with glioblastoma, he pivoted into biopharma to fight cancer and eventually sold his biotech company for $21 billion.
person:robert dugen.zero_start_advice_en: Focus on making money and future success rather than worrying about losing money, find a genuinely knowledgeable mentor, and put business and financial literacy first. Stay passionate and action-oriented, refuse anxious overthinking, push through failure, and keep creating value.

person:grant mitt.first_money_or_break_en: Starting out reselling sneakers, selling on eBay, and working sales at DirecTV and Walmart, he dollar-cost averaged $500-$1,000 weekly into Bitcoin, Ethereum, and quality stocks to become a millionaire at 24. He later built the solar company Met Group from scratch, reaching roughly $30 million in annual revenue.
person:grant mitt.zero_start_advice_en: First assess whether you are better suited to founding a company or being an intrapreneur at a great one, and avoid premature diversification early on. Pick an industry poised for growth over the next 20 years, build hardcore communication skills through high-volume cold calling and door-to-door sales, and diversify only after dominating one thing and making your first fortune.

person:myron golden.first_money_or_break_en: After starting as a garbage collector earning $6.25 an hour and being inspired at 16 by his father leaving a job to go independent, he made his first $1 million at 45 only to lose it all from premature lifestyle inflation and family setbacks. He bounced back by investing heavily in mentors to master one-to-many stage selling and shifting from trading time to building assets, eventually reaching $15 million a year.
person:myron golden.zero_start_advice_en: Reject "get rich in 90 days" deadline goals that cause discouragement and quitting when unmet, and start by solving real pain points for others. Use free high-value content to earn attention, offer high-ticket solutions to high-net-worth buyers who can pay, and pay to enter higher-level rooms to learn and network.

person:todd graves.first_money_or_break_en: After working in restaurants through high school and college, his business plan received the lowest grade in his class and every local bank rejected his loan, so he went alone to Alaska, lived in a tent, and worked commercial fishing to save about $50,000. Combining that with a $50,000 SBA small business loan, he renovated a rundown storefront by hand and founded Raising Cane's in 1996.
person:todd graves.zero_start_advice_en: Starting over with nothing, he would return to the familiar restaurant industry, find another addictive breakout single item, perfect that one focus, build a team around it, and scale. When you have no money and cannot borrow, raise seed capital through physical labor and leverage government and mentor resources like SBA loans, SBDC, and SCORE.

person:big vic tip.first_money_or_break_en: With only a high school diploma, in his 20s after losing both parents to cancer and going through a divorce while raising two young kids with credit card debt, he founded Blackstone Medical Services in 2012 in pajamas from his kitchen using one Apple computer. Raising money from friends and family, emailing insurers daily for partnerships, and pitching doctors in person, he moved into a $500-a-month office and surpassed industry giants by 2019 to become number one in the U.S. by order volume.
person:big vic tip.zero_start_advice_en: Climbing back from a $78 low starts with truly making up your mind, willing to sacrifice everything (including sleep and time) and never quitting. Practically, take big entrepreneurial risks to build a real business generating strong cash flow and revenue for years, spending your first 30 years learning, your middle 30 years earning, and your final 30 years giving back.

person:lavon perrin.first_money_or_break_en: He started out selling long-distance phone service at MCI, becoming one of its youngest supervisors, and later worked as a private chauffeur for celebrities. During the pandemic, he returned to the insurance industry, became a top underwriter, and built his own insurance agency team.
person:lavon perrin.zero_start_advice_en: Carry almost blind confidence and ambition, take action first, figure out the numbers along the way, and keep pushing forward. You do not have to start with your passion; work in a lucrative field to build the capital that funds your dreams, and spend your youth experimenting, traveling, and saving, because you cannot lose if you never quit.

person:andy elliott.first_money_or_break_en: Growing up poor and earning D grades in school, he entered the zero-barrier sales industry at 19, making $125,000 in year one, $225,000 in year two, and $500,000 in year three at age 20. He later founded a major sales training company generating $160 million in annual revenue.
person:andy elliott.zero_start_advice_en: Break into sales, where there is no barrier to entry, and master both selling and leadership while turning rock-bottom pain into fuel to bounce back. Focus completely on your clients, care about their interests even more than they do, believe deeply in yourself, and refuse mediocrity.

person:todd nepola.first_money_or_break_en: He entered wealthy circles early by washing cars and boats for the rich, then saved a six-figure nest egg from commissions as a stockbroker in the 1990s. At 25, he emptied his account down to $50 to buy his first commercial property for $575,000, renovated and leased it, refinanced at an $800,000 valuation within seven months to pull out all his principal, and secured $5,000 a month in permanent free cash flow.
person:todd nepola.zero_start_advice_en: Do not buy into the traditional script of getting good grades, finding a safe job, saving, paying off a mortgage, and retiring. First believe you are no different from wealthy people, put yourself around the richest people (such as valeting at a country club), find self-made role models to emulate, and work twice as hard thinking about how to create value for others.

person:giannis antetokounmpo.first_money_or_break_en: Raised in a poor immigrant family in Athens, Greece, he sold CDs, watches, and DVDs on the street until ages 16-17 to help support his family. While earning just $300 a month with his club, he received a 5,000-euro contract offer at 14 (turning down Adidas for Nike after insisting his brother be signed too) and was drafted by the NBA's Milwaukee Bucks in 2013.
person:giannis antetokounmpo.zero_start_advice_en: Starting out does not require much seed money if you stay sharp and resourceful. Teach yourself financial literacy early (by reading books like "Rich Dad Poor Dad" and "The Psychology of Money"), stay intensely disciplined with positive self-talk, stay humble enough to find mentors and learn from anyone, and invest your earnings in the market to compound.

person:doug williams.first_money_or_break_en: After graduating in computer science, he started as a frontline programmer writing device-communication software on site for projects like the B1 bomber and Disney, gaining protocol expertise and client-facing skills. He rose to partner at Andersen running healthcare technology, later led IBM's global healthcare consulting practice, served as COO of healthcare company HMS Holdings (sold for $3.5 billion), and now works as an early-stage VC and board director.
person:doug williams.zero_start_advice_en: Stop obsessing over how to get ahead and ask instead, "What can I do to help others?" Focus on mastering and enjoying your current role while genuinely caring for and lifting up colleagues and partners, because when you consistently help others succeed, champions and opportunities naturally come back to you.

person:justin waller.first_money_or_break_en: Broke at age 24 in Louisiana, he landed a steel-building erection contract and used it to secure his first $15,000 bank line of credit. With a weekly payroll of roughly $2,500 and two employees building backyard structures, he launched his business from there.
person:justin waller.zero_start_advice_en: Once you pick a direction, start immediately and commit relentlessly to one core business without quitting halfway, selling with conviction backed by belief in your product and delivery. Spend your 20s staying sober and disciplined (no smoking or drinking), build physical strength to command respect, ignore naysayers, and join a circle of driven peers.

person:shaquille oneal.first_money_or_break_en: Raised in poverty, he built his initial capital from high NBA salaries and endorsement deals. After blowing his first $1 million in 30 minutes, he taught himself finance and leveraged his sports income into investments and franchises (at one point owning 155 Five Guys locations), building a vast business empire.
person:shaquille oneal.zero_start_advice_en: Write your plans down first, then find people already succeeding at something similar, study and borrow their playbook, and add your own unique style. Business will always have ups and downs, so if you never lose faith, you will reach the top faster.

person:ann malum.first_money_or_break_en: With a negative net worth at ages 26-27, she first founded the homeless-aid nonprofit Back on My Feet before spotting an early gap in boutique Pilates and launching Solidcore. Expanding purely by word of mouth with zero marketing spend for the first four years, she sold the company nine and a half years later at a valuation over $300 million, cashing out roughly $90 million for her equity.
person:ann malum.zero_start_advice_en: Build a business around a unique skill where you outperform 95% of people combined with an area you love. Instead of leaving cash in a bank for tiny interest, learn investing through books and podcasts and put even as little as $1,000 into the stock market (such as index funds) early to capture compounding.

person:barbara corcoran.first_money_or_break_en: After holding 22 jobs including waitressing, she borrowed $1,000 at age 21 to found New York residential brokerage The Corcoran Group, later turning down a $2 million buyout before selling the company two years later for $66 million in cash. She later wrote a persuasive letter to win back her seat on Shark Tank.
person:barbara corcoran.zero_start_advice_en: Start humbly from scratch (like selling apples on a street corner to make your first $50,000 and snowball from there), do what you genuinely love, stay authentic, and use communication well. Once you have savings, buy a two-family home early so you can live in one unit and use the rent to pay the mortgage.

person:glenn boyd.first_money_or_break_en: Born into a poor family and self-taught in programming as a teen, he quit his job in his early 20s and survived startup life on his last $1,000 and the sale of his motorcycle. After building LAN security-auditing software that won the Federal Reserve and major U.S. banks to reach $1 million a year, he pivoted into web traffic marketing analytics, scaled to $120 million in revenue within four years, went public in 1999, and ultimately sold for over $1 billion.
person:glenn boyd.zero_start_advice_en: Tech newcomers should target fast-growing cybersecurity, while anyone with $100,000 in seed capital can start a service business for fast cash flow or spend a full year building a product if they have technical skills. Choose a field you love enough to stick with for 3-5+ years, stay in areas you know, and keep cash reserves to buy cheap or position yourself during recessions.

person:reid hoffman.first_money_or_break_en: Raised in a civil-servant family, he graduated from Stanford in AI and worked at Apple and Fujitsu to build product skills and connections before launching his first startup, Social (which did not succeed but got him on the entrepreneurial track). He then played a core role at PayPal (acquired by eBay for $1.5 billion) and founded LinkedIn in 2003, eventually selling it to Microsoft for $26 billion and becoming a billionaire around age 38.
person:reid hoffman.zero_start_advice_en: Do something radically different from what most people are doing. Avoid playing one-year short-term games and instead compound your thinking over 10-year horizons (such as founding an AI cancer drug discovery company) to achieve industry-disrupting breakthroughs through long-term accumulation.

person:ben mala.first_money_or_break_en: Starting out poor in his early 20s, he first worked for wealthy people and partnered with them to expand his perspective. He then used a VA loan with zero down payment to buy his first 1-4 unit multifamily property, gradually scaling from affordable housing into retail properties and hotels.
person:ben mala.zero_start_advice_en: First get a job with steady income to qualify for bank loan pre-approval, then use a zero-down VA loan or a 3.5%-down FHA loan to buy a 2-4 unit multifamily property where rent covers your bills or generates positive cash flow. Cut out partying and vanity spending, carefully analyze good deals, lean on professionals, and stack assets piece by piece according to plan.

person:edwin aave.first_money_or_break_en: Born into poverty and placed in foster care after his parents went to prison, he began supporting his family at age 15. At 21, he quit a $70,000-a-year job to launch a home security company, buying a van ahead of time to build a door-to-door sales team and pushing hard to fulfill a promise to buy his mother a house within 90 days.
person:edwin aave.zero_start_advice_en: First clarify the core "why" driving you, find an industry capable of paying your target income, and partner with a successful mentor whose incentives align with yours. Break big goals down to the finest detail with strict deadlines, act before you have all the resources, and split income into thirds to protect cash reserves.

person:muhammad binghatti.first_money_or_break_en: Spending 16 to 17 years in real estate development, he compensated for limited early capital by crafting a highly recognizable, unified architectural design language that turned every building into a free billboard. He went on to develop the world's first Bugatti, Mercedes-Benz, and Jacob & Co branded luxury residences, scaling the company into the multi-billion-dollar range.
person:muhammad binghatti.zero_start_advice_en: Master sales and marketing with a strong focus on digital marketing, and when resources are tight, make the product itself unmistakable so it spreads organically. Avoid jumping blindly into unrelated industries like restaurants or juice factories; stay focused on one core lane and expand through vertical integration.

person:eric spofford.first_money_or_break_en: Having started dealing drugs at age 10, he got clean at 21 and founded an addiction treatment center from scratch at 23. Thirteen years later, he sold the business to a private equity-backed strategic buyer for $115 million alongside roughly $40 million in underlying real estate.
person:eric spofford.zero_start_advice_en: First generate cash flow through a practical business or high-income sales role and resist the urge to blow it immediately on luxury living. Instead, channel profits into appreciating assets that produce recurring passive cash flow (like Section 8 housing), building a continuous "money stream" rather than a one-time "money pile."

person:tony buzbee.first_money_or_break_en: After leaving the Marine Corps, he attended law school in Houston and joined a top law firm earning roughly $250,000 a year. He then resigned decisively to launch his own practice out of a small suburban storefront with two employees, scaling through major courtroom wins and reputation to a 150-person firm.
person:tony buzbee.zero_start_advice_en: Know your strengths and weaknesses and commit to continuous self-improvement, including reading a book every week. Stay locked into a core high-margin lane without getting distracted, and when you know in your gut you are right, move forward boldly without self-doubt.

person:brent franklin.first_money_or_break_en: After military service he scraped by mowing lawns before a friend got him work on oil rigs in Midland-Odessa, Texas. A few years later he bought drilling equipment, spent over a decade wholesaling and flipping houses to build capital, and ultimately built a vertically integrated oil, gas, and investment company.
person:brent franklin.zero_start_advice_en: Find what you excel at, monetize solving a real pain point, and invest heavily in social media marketing to establish your brand and point of view. Cut ties decisively with people on a different wavelength, pay to get into successful circles, ignore skeptics, and chase your dream relentlessly.

clip:V6I3R5Z-YZI:0.first_money_or_break_en: Starting his first venture at 16, he left his poor hometown at 18 to go all-in on sales, moving up from a frontline rep to sales manager in solar. He dropped out at 19, built a multimillion-dollar business by 20, and eventually founded a major residential solar company.
clip:V6I3R5Z-YZI:0.zero_start_advice_en: Invest in yourself first to learn high-value skills like sales and marketing, and save enough to leave an impoverished environment for a major city full of opportunity and wealth. Raise your own value before networking upward, cut out draining friends, and never give up.

person:mike kessner.first_money_or_break_en: After quitting a Chicago recruiting job after one month due to brutal winters and early mornings, he gained experience at a large firm in St. Louis before returning home to care for his widowed mother and entering commercial insurance sales as a producer. After 3-4 years of trial and error, he stuck with it for over 25 years, scaling the firm into a 2,000-person PE roll-up and selling it before joining Virtus Insurance as a partner and head of sales.
person:mike kessner.zero_start_advice_en: If his bank account hit zero tomorrow, he would immediately take a full-time sales role and out-hustle and outwork everyone to earn commission checks quickly. From there, he would diversify across stocks, real estate, private equity/startups, and collectible hobbies he genuinely knows and loves.

person:alex kaufman.first_money_or_break_en: Getting sober at 21, he worked as an $8.50-an-hour fast-food worker and dishwasher before moving into oil and gas. In December 2018, he and his childhood friend Matt each put in $28,000 to buy their first property in North Austin for around $139,000, later cashing out $150,000 and building a long-term portfolio of roughly 100 units plus a co-founded real estate brokerage.
person:alex kaufman.zero_start_advice_en: Make zero excuses, because if you want it badly enough you will find a way and accept the sacrifices. Cut unnecessary spending and indulgences, tune out limiting beliefs from others and society, take 100% responsibility for yourself, and keep compounding earnings into real estate and your business.

person:anastasia soare.first_money_or_break_en: Having immigrated to the U.S. from Romania broke and speaking no English, she started Anastasia Beverly Hills in 1997 by solving her own eyebrow-grooming pain point. She sold the company in 2018 at a $3 billion valuation after previously holding 100% ownership.
person:anastasia soare.zero_start_advice_en: Do not be afraid to start and stay confident, avoid spending recklessly early on to show off, and watch cash flow and profit closely while constantly reinvesting earnings. At the same time, embrace new shifts like social media and AI.

person:jesse itzler.first_money_or_break_en: At 23, sleeping on a friend's couch while barely getting by on $16,000 a year, he failed at ventures selling seafood door-to-door, records, T-shirts, and marketing before spotting an opportunity after being invited onto a private jet. He co-founded a private aviation company that reached over $5 billion in annual sales and sold to Buffett, becoming a millionaire at 26.
person:jesse itzler.zero_start_advice_en: When you have no connections, go every day to top venues like the Beverly Hills Hotel to create proximity to major players. Stay hungry, and be prepared to grind patiently over a decade to build wealth slowly.

person:dom does deals.zero_start_advice_en: With zero capital, start by driving for dollars to spot rundown or vacant properties, which requires no real estate license. Build initial capital through wholesaling contracts to avoid renovation debt, and partner with experienced teams to help close deals.

clip:qQIKf7YQBbA:0.first_money_or_break_en: Starting out saddled with $20 million in debt after his father's bankruptcy, he worked his way up in hospitality from bussing tables to the boardroom. He eventually founded Diamond Resorts International and sold it to Hilton.

person:aliko dangote.first_money_or_break_en: Starting out selling candy to classmates as a student and later trading commodities like cement, sugar, and coal, he saw Asia being built by its own people and pivoted to backward integration by building local African factories for imported essentials. That strategy created a vast industrial empire spanning cement, fertilizer, and the world's largest single-train oil refinery.
person:aliko dangote.zero_start_advice_en: Be honest, humble, and disciplined, and execute with sharp strategy and focus. Master essential physical industries, know your sector inside out, treat the customer as king, and never lose heart through life and health setbacks.

person:marcus lemonis.first_money_or_break_en: Raised in a blue-collar family, he worked hard at school and realized early that while he lacked athletic or artistic talent, he excelled at math and money. Becoming a millionaire at 27, he built a public RV-industry company generating $900 million in annual net profit and acquired Bed Bath & Beyond.
person:marcus lemonis.zero_start_advice_en: Always keep ample cash reserves to seize opportunities, reject flashy spending in favor of living modestly at home while keeping the business rich, and reinvest profits into employees and operations. Stay humble, curious, and open to learning from others rather than acting like a know-it-all, and put employees first in an inverted-pyramid service culture.

clip:uUwf3HM_bBg:0.first_money_or_break_en: The son of a plumber, he built everything from scratch after three consecutive business failures at ages 18, 19, and 22, setting up a Venice Beach booth in 1981 with $200. Inspired by dental filling gel, he invented gel nails and continuously reinvested high-margin profits to expand into 90 countries, surpassing $100 million in annual revenue.
clip:uUwf3HM_bBg:0.zero_start_advice_en: Sell yourself well first, avoid debt, continuously reinvest high-margin profits, expand globally early, and refuse to quit even after repeated failures. At the same time, build the habit of saving money instead of squandering it.

person:abdulla kudrath.first_money_or_break_en: During medical aid work in East Africa, he realized one doctor alone could only treat surface symptoms, so he returned home to study operations and used his medical savings to open his first urgent care center. He went on to expand into over seven businesses spanning physician groups, real estate development, and luxury car rentals.
person:abdulla kudrath.zero_start_advice_en: Save diligently first for seed capital, calculate your risks with backup plans, and overcome the fear of loss and poverty to launch boldly. Build character traits like discipline, trustworthiness, and execution first so you can actually capture and keep wealth.

person:andy frisella.first_money_or_break_en: Dropping out after one semester of college with no investors or family inheritance, he opened his first supplement retail store in Springfield, Missouri with $12,000, making just $7 on day one; unprofitable for three years and averaging only $695 a month from years three to ten while sleeping in the store and bartending on the side, he did not open a second store until year six. Rejected in 2012 by the world's largest supplement distributor, he built a fully vertically integrated supply chain and grew it into a multibillion-dollar enterprise.
person:andy frisella.zero_start_advice_en: Entrepreneurship is nothing like the polished version online, as the real journey is grueling and difficult; hitting obstacles means you are on the right path, not doing it wrong. Anyone can earn skills, resilience, and grit by paying the price, staying disciplined, taking consistent action, and hiring experts where they lack knowledge.

clip:VW2t21zzYl8:3.first_money_or_break_en: Born into a poor New Orleans family, he was homeless at 13 and sentenced to 10 years in prison at 16, where he began reading voraciously and studying investing and ownership. After his release, he built wealth through U.S. stock trading (including a $1.1 million single-day gain ahead of Nvidia's stock split), operating businesses, and commercial real estate, becoming a millionaire around age 35 and earning eight figures annually at his peak.
clip:VW2t21zzYl8:3.zero_start_advice_en: Stop trading only time for money and change your situation by reading widely and executing relentlessly. Invest in leading U.S. tech companies (in AI and cybersecurity) for ownership, use commercial real estate and charitable structures to legally reduce taxes, and establish family SOPs to pass down knowledge.

person:stephen cloobeck.first_money_or_break_en: After early shopping-center development losses when contractors and tenants went bankrupt, at 29 he partnered with his father in Las Vegas to build Polo Towers, the world's largest timeshare resort, on time and on budget. Overcoming a negative $20 million starting position, he grew his hospitality business to 435 hotels across 35 countries before selling it to Hilton at a $3.3 billion enterprise value.
person:stephen cloobeck.zero_start_advice_en: Do deep due diligence and personally master every part of the business while keeping startup agility inside a large organization. Treat banks, investors, and your team with total integrity and transparency, listen closely to customer needs, and never quit when told no.

clip:1ZcDMQp8w0E:0.first_money_or_break_en: Raised by a mother earning just $30,000 a year while supporting five children, she lived in a 700-square-foot apartment with four roommates in college and launched a soap and feminine hygiene brand with just $67. She made her first $1 million in year one and grew it past $20 million (eight figures) in annual revenue within eight years.
clip:1ZcDMQp8w0E:0.zero_start_advice_en: Enter an unsexy, high-frequency essential niche and earn strong word of mouth through authentic content and organic traffic before running ads. Company revenue is not personal spending money, so live minimally early on, reinvest all profits, and keep a tight grip on your financial books.

clip:7Cxfg0N_MUw:0.first_money_or_break_en: With zero dollars in his bank account at age 19, he founded the e-commerce clothing brand For The Low Clothing. He gained early traction by dominating social media exposure through rapid weekly product drops and iteration.
clip:7Cxfg0N_MUw:0.zero_start_advice_en: Borrow $10,000 in startup capital from friends in your network and run a fast-cash offline business like auto detailing to build your bankroll before moving back into online digital ventures.

person:johnny anton.first_money_or_break_en: From an Iraqi immigrant family, he grew up in a poor Detroit neighborhood and spent two years homeless before turning things around through high-ticket commission-only sales, earning $500,000 in annual commissions by age 24. Leading a team that doubled company revenue to nearly nine figures in two years, he made his first fortune and became an eight-figure millionaire.
person:johnny anton.zero_start_advice_en: Start by selling for a company with the highest-ticket offer to cover rent and basic living costs quickly, then use your skills to deliver free value for others to build reputation and case studies. Once you land a flagship client, sell high-value, low-risk paid offers to their direct competitors, then build a sales team and scale with paid traffic.

person:jacob hopkins.first_money_or_break_en: After side hustles in auto detailing, dropshipping, and real estate stalled since high school, including losing $3,000 to $4,000 a month in real estate, he dropped out of college at 19 with over $10,000 in debt. Guided by Alex Hormozi into a sales role at Gym Launch, he made 200 to 400 calls a day (far outpacing the 100-call norm), caught up to top veterans within two to three weeks, and grew his income to over $250,000 a year.
